paper.title: Association of Physical Activity With Risk of Mortality Among Breast Cancer Survivors
paper.authors: Chen LH, Irwin MR, Olmstead R, Haque R.

study.population: Postmenopausal breast cancer survivors diagnosed 2 or more years prior, enrolled in a California health plan between 1996 and 2012, followed until death or study end.

exposure.definition: Categorized as active, moderately active, or insufficiently active using the Godin-Shephard Leisure-Time Physical Activity Questionnaire at baseline

outcome.name: All-cause mortality
outcome.definition: Death from any cause ascertained via health plan and state/national death databases

missing_confounders.rationale: Existing heart disease limits physical capacity and predicts higher all-cause mortality, potentially confounding the activity-mortality link.

bias_risks.explanation: Women who report higher activity may also engage in other health-promoting behaviors (e.g., better diet, adherence to medication) that lower mortality independent of activity.
Physical activity was assessed once at baseline using a self‑report questionnaire, likely leading to non‑differential misclassification that biases the hazard ratio toward the null.
Important confounders such as socioeconomic status, BMI, and smoking were not measured, so the observed association may partly reflect these unmeasured factors.
Loss to follow‑up could differ by health status; sicker survivors may be more likely to discontinue plan membership, distorting the activity‑mortality relationship.
Exposure was defined at cohort entry (baseline) after a minimum 2‑year survival period, so there is no evident period where outcome could not occur before exposure classification.

critique.overall_assessment: The study controlled for a broad set of clinical and psychosocial confounders, which strengthens the causal interpretation. However, the lack of key socioeconomic, behavioral, and cardiovascular variables, combined with potential measurement error in self‑reported activity and possible healthy‑user bias, means the observed hazard ratio may be inflated. Consequently, the evidence suggests a protective association but should be interpreted cautiously pending further validation.
